title: Why does everything feel so joyless? Welcome to the age of decadence without pleasure
excerpt: Decadence in our era comes in technologically mediated forms, emptied of desire and obsessed with self-optimisation
content_html:
Do you want to have a good time? You know, really enjoy yourself? Click here, and tell us your desires. Maybe it’s a new outfit, or some exotic cuisine delivered anonymously and steaming hot to your door. Maybe it’s porn or gambling. Perhaps you prefer the infinite scroll, the endlessly unfurling ribbon of glossy images and videos starring people you’ll never meet doing things you’ll never do. Or maybe you favor talking to a chatbot who will assure you that you are the most special of all its users.

For anyone with an Internet connection and a little discretionary income, the contemporary moment offers a superabundance of seductive distractions. Why then the pervasive mood of emptiness? Why are so many at once overstimulated and bored?

Welcome to the era of decadence without pleasure.

The concept of decadence as a marker of cultural decline coinciding with a high level of wealth has been around since the twilight of the ancient Greeks and Romans. After the Roman emperor Elagabalus took the throne at 14, he served flamingo brains, seasoned his food with pearls, and, according to one account, smothered guests to death with an avalanche of rose petals. But his vices were outdone by Nero, who had his enemies sewn into wild animal skins and devoured by dogs in an elaborate garden spectacle.

So decadence has an inescapably pejorative ring, suggesting decay, excess and a falling away from norms and ideals. Critics of decadence have usually hailed from the political right, and the same is true today: consider conservative New York Times columnist Ross Douthat’s critique of cultural and economic stagnation in his 2020 book The Decadent Society, or billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s complaints about faltering innovation and the supposed decline of the west. JD Vance likes to invoke the fall of Rome, warning, in his 2026 memoir Communion, that the US is “a great civilization” tumbling into “disrepair”. But plenty of thinkers on the left also worry that modern wealthy societies have entered a period of paralysis, under the shadow of what the Italian theorist Franco “Bifo” Berardi calls “the slow cancellation of the future”.

That all sounds bad. Yet a passionate minority has sometimes found, in decadence, reasons for hope. Cultures later judged decadent produced extraordinary upwellings of art, like the flare of a dying star. Think of the undulating arabesques of Rococo painting before the French Revolution, or the lush shimmering silks of the late Ottomans, or the experimental cinema and nightlife of Weimar Berlin.

Nowhere was the cultural potential of decadence more visible than in the late-19th century. In France, Britain and (with less gusto) in the United States, artists such as Oscar Wilde, Aubrey Beardsley, Joris-Karl Huysmans and Rachilde developed new literary and visual styles championing extravagance, sensuousness and the superiority of artifice. It is to these avant-garde experiments that we owe green carnations (the fakest of flowers), frivolous dandies obsessed with perfumes, a bejeweled tortoise crushed to death by the weight of its splendor, and erotic nightmares including a woman with monstrous flowers growing between her thighs and a male anatomical model whose legs spread at the click of a spring so that he can be penetrated by his female lover. Such taboo-busting grotesquery protested against the inertia of modern civilization by applying moral and aesthetic shock treatment.

The decadents, however, were not just provocateurs. Their revolt against Victorian society’s deadening enslavement to usefulness, materialism and conventionality put forward a positive philosophy of life, a certain way of thinking about pleasure. Against their era’s obsession with use-value and profit, the decadents insisted that pleasure was, or ought to be, “useless”, enjoyed for its own sake in life’s passing moments. “Not the fruit of experience, but experience itself, is the end,” intoned the essayist Walter Pater, one of the guiding lights of English decadence, in his masterpiece The Renaissance. A reclusive Oxford don, Pater was said to have once stopped High Street traffic to stroke a cat. Why? For the sensation of fur beneath his fingers. The virtue of decadent pleasure is that it is useless, an end in itself.

The fixations of fin-de-siècle decadence that inspired Oscar Wilde and company are still with us, but in shrivelled, technologically mediated forms. GLP-1s turn the delights of eating into a problem to be managed. Anti-ageing remedies and “looksmaxxing” turn decadence’s preoccupation with self-styling into a (literally painful) form of self-optimisation. AI restages decadence’s love of artifice by outsourcing human thinking to a chatty, eager-to-please machine butler.

The problem with contemporary culture isn’t that we’re too decadent. We have inherited the surfaces of decadence – luxury, excess, artifice, bodily display – but have surrendered the fin de siècle’s commitment to pleasure. The result is a culture in which pleasure is subordinated to programs of optimisation and replaced at scale by numbing algorithmic stimulation and promises of instant gratification. Whether you’re after goods, food, art or ideas, you can get more, faster, now.

But quantity and speed can’t make up for the paradox at the heart of today’s decadence: the fact that it’s often “meh” and oddly joyless. It’s a sign of the times that this spring, Amazon’s Chinese rival launched in the UK and Europe under a name that promises to deliver emotional fulfilment: Joybuy.

The ‘looksmaxxing’ era

Bryan Johnson, the frequently shirtless tech tycoon who has funnelled his fortune into what he calls the “Don’t Die” movement, has turned his quest for immortality into a prolonged exhibition of ascetic self-management. His lifestyle is harrowingly spartan: he doesn’t drink alcohol, avoids the sun, never goes out in the evening, and subsists primarily on lentils, boiled broccoli and macadamia nuts. Yet his regimen is, in its peculiar way, one of prurient excess. He swallows up to 111 pills a day, tracks his night-time erections, and once tapped his teenage son for blood plasma. His fight against death costs a reported $2m a year.

Johnson presents himself as a man of the future, but he has a 19th-century double. While pallid, faintly androgynous men with money and strange habits are not rare in decadent literature, the most famous is Duke Jean des Esseintes, the hero of Joris-Karl Huysmans’s 1884 novel Against the Grain, a work considered the Bible of decadence. The last scion of an aristocratic French family, des Esseintes creates for himself a cloistered world of voluptuous artifice: padded walls, rare books, exotic flowers, fragrant bonbons, subtle liqueurs, perfumes so sweet they verge on rancid.

Like Johnson, des Esseintes is medically fragile, obsessed with death, and preoccupied with the minutiae of his private sensations. Like Johnson, he sees his retreat from ordinary society into a tightly controlled artificial environment as an experiment that tests the limits of human possibility. But whereas des Esseintes’s withdrawal is an immersion into the subtleties of sensation, Johnson’s “Don’t Die” movement treats the delights of the senses as suspect, even fatal. Des Esseintes hosts a funeral banquet for his “dead virility” in a dining room draped in black, opening on to charcoaled gardens, with guests dining on black-bordered plates filled with black food (rye bread, caviar, black pudding, cuts of meat dripping with liquorice-coloured sauce). Johnson, by contrast, treats impotence as a technical problem, repeatedly shocking his penis to increase his erections.

Johnson’s programme is extreme, but he is not an anomaly. His lifestyle makes visible, in exaggerated form, new attitudes toward pleasure and embodiment being pushed by today’s tech billionaires. While some superwealthy people in or around Palo Alto are biohacking for longevity with the help of concierge medics, others are treating even sexual pleasure as a domain to be perfected through medical interventions. For example, at Dr Sally Greenwald’s exclusive OB-GYN practice, nicknamed the “Billionaire’s Vagina Club” – Greenwald describes her clientele as “the top 0.001%” – middle-aged women can improve their “sexspan” through bespoke advice, hormonal cocktails and tracking devices. “Sex equals sleep, stress reduction, cardiovascular engagement, relational fulfilment, and pelvic-floor health, and each of those equals health,” Greenwald says.

These attitudes reflect the fantasies of a narrow elite obsessed with human enhancement and – above all else – the prolongation of their own survival. The class politics of pleasureless decadence can be roughly summarized as: biohacking and quantified asceticism for the rich, algorithmic stimulation for the rest.

In contexts of extreme inequality, rich people tend to set the terms by which pleasure is understood and experienced. The very fact of inequality injures pleasure, because in a stratified society, food, art, travel and other delights can devolve into occasions to demonstrate rank or taste. Our present social order, however, is not just radically unequal; it’s dominated by a ruling class that distrusts pleasure and sensation. What passes for “fun” among today’s top 0.001% amounts to anything but: think of the 80-hour workweeks championed by tech titans like Elon Musk, or Equinox gym’s “Optimize” longevity membership costing $40,000 a year, or courtside seats at Knicks games inside the miniature surveillance state that is Madison Square Garden. And because of their outsized political and cultural influence, their sway over public and private investment, and their habit of not paying their share of tax, the pleasurelessness of the ultra-monied classes trickles down to the rest of us.

“I think trying to optimise things … is actually the divine spark within us,” recently professed the German biotech billionaire Christian Angermayer, a champion of “humanmaxxing”, the use of drugs and supplements to enhance the body. Divinity aside, it seems pertinent to mention that the person content with every day sensations makes for a poor consumer. But get people outside the plutocratic class to reconceive their minds and bodies as sites of perpetual self-improvement, and you have, in Angermayer’s words, “a total addressable market of ideally 100%”.

The most culturally revealing such market is for GLP-1s such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro. One in eight American adults report taking GLP-1 injectables for weight loss, according to a 2025 Gallup poll, and far more express interest in taking them. The global market for this class of drugs is expected to reach $190bn by 2035. For many, these medications confer real benefits. Yet it seems fair to ask: what does the widespread embrace of appetite-governing pharmaceuticals suggest about our culture’s handling of pleasure and desire?

GLP-1s reshape the felt relation between desire and satisfaction, as research has already begun to show. While more studies are needed, some users report a diminution of pleasure across several areas of their lives: they complain of lethargy, decreased libido, emotional flatness and a weakened connection to the social dimensions of eating.

The decadence of the fin de siècle celebrated cornucopian abundance. Take for example Aubrey Beardsley’s 1896 drawing The Fruit Bearers, depicting two figures bearing colossal bowls of fruit, lush grapes overhanging, a peacock in the background observing the opulent procession. In contrast, today’s anhedonic decadence celebrates the inhibition, even the transcendence, of appetite. While in haute cuisine the trappings of indulgence are preserved – some upmarket eateries now offer “small appetite” menus featuring caviar and foie gras – the tendency is toward delicate minimalism. Because eating is a quintessentially communal activity, an intervention in how people eat is also an intervention in how we socialize.

It seems reasonable to expect, meanwhile, that the widespread uptake of such drugs may contribute to a tightening not just of belts but of beauty norms. Looksmaxxing, an online subculture aimed primarily at young men, presents a darker strain of physical perfectionism, treating the body as a site of correction. Of course, women have long been ground down by painful and impossible beauty standards. What’s striking about looksmaxxing is the migration of this kind of disciplinary logic into a male subculture that speaks of beauty in terms of brutal domination: anyone can be “mogged” (outshone by a more handsome man), and one of the purposes of maxxing is to increase one’s “sexual market value”. Key to this subculture is the rejection of subjective taste in favor of mathematical norms (looksmaxxers prize certain ratios of facial proportion, measuring, for instance, the height of the forehead or the distance between the pupils).

“[T]o make oneself beautiful is a universal instinct,” a young Max Beerbohm wrote in his 1894 essay A Defence of Cosmetics, a send-up of decadence’s cult of artifice. Whereas the fin-de-siècle decadents with their love of makeup treated the face as a mask to play with or an enigma to contemplate, looksmaxxers recast the face as a set of homogenizing metrics requiring arduous correction. “The men are weeping in the gym,” writes Andrew McMillan in his prescient 2015 poem about punitive male beauty standards:

they have got too close to the glass

and now they are laying

in the broken pools of their own faces.

The pleasureless decadence machine

The fin de siècle had its own cult of masculine self-display in the form of the dandy, with his carefully tailored coat, polished shoes and pigskin gloves. The dandy’s concern for appearance was just part of the era’s wide-ranging love of stylization. “The first duty in life is to be as artificial as possible,” Oscar Wilde proclaimed. “What the second duty is no one has yet discovered.” Wilde and other decadents prized the made over the natural. Artifice was a way of intensifying the given world, overlaying the hard facts of life with a glittering sheen or a more pleasant smell. After all, what is the dandy’s perfume but a victory for pleasure over necessity?

AI marks a triumph of artifice more sweeping than the old decadents could have imagined. Yet far from bolstering our capacity for perceptual intensity, AI presents new threats to both. Its productions – LinkedIn posts about the virtues of entrepreneurship, cartoon soap operas about the infidelities of anthropomorphized fruits – are eerily hollow, with no felt experience, embodiment or sensation behind them. AI is the pleasureless decadence machine.

Already our algorithmically driven culture is saturated with a deluge of slop that promises numbing, empty stimulation. The old decadents were fascinated by the prospect of mental oblivion, the loss of self-control in the face of overwhelming beauty. Today, AI researchers warn of “human enfeeblement” as tech companies seek to draw users into relations of dependency and infantilization, with machines to do their “thinking” for them.

While the fin-de-siècle left imprints on visual art, fashion, music and other art forms, it was primarily as a literary movement that its decadence made cultural interventions. Crucial to decadent writing was a taste for language – lilting rhythms, overheated exclamations – that would affect the reader viscerally, leaving her trembling, her moral assumptions upended. In contrast, LLMs leach language of pleasure by blandifying it: the algorithm steers language away from the idiosyncratic and toward the predictable.

Pleasure isn’t just about hedonism or indulgence in “useless” objects. It is one of the principal ways we, as embodied beings, perceive value. Pain teaches us not to touch the hot stove twice; pleasure guides us toward the sweetness of clean water and fresh air. Pleasure is not infallible: some things that feel good are cruel, addictive, or destructive. But the embodied experience of pleasure is crucial to how we learn and how we make judgments about what is good, beautiful and worth pursuing. These are not judgments we can wisely cede to disembodied machines.

“There is no pleasure or pain for an AI, no skin in the game,” the philosopher Carissa Véliz writes in her recent book Prophecy. As a result, an AI “cannot care, and therefore cannot value”. Without some felt relation to pleasure and pain, judgments of value and taste become abstract and bloodless.

Reclaiming everyday pleasures

Because of its commitment to embodied pleasure, fin-de-siècle decadence offers powerful lessons for the increasingly disembodied, tech-optimised world championed by elites. This is not to suggest, however, that the old decadents were living uncomplicated lives of satisfaction and joy. WB Yeats called the poets of 1890s London “the tragic generation”. The decadents could be moody and morbid, susceptible to ennui, spleen and other Baudelairean ailments. In other words, they were all too human. Some died young, succumbing to alcoholism or tuberculosis; others abandoned the religion of art to join the Catholic church. Fin-de-siècle decadence had, moreover, an aristocratic and misogynistic bent. Many of its most influential English champions were highly educated men who regarded ordinary life with aloofness, even contempt.

From the start, however, decadence was both an elite and a minoritarian movement, spearheaded largely by men (and some women) of privilege – but responsible for injecting a new awareness of queerness into public consciousness.

Oscar Wilde’s 1890 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray is a story of a thrill-seeker’s descent into decadent squalor – hedonism, moral bankruptcy, irresponsible self-indulgence and the exploitation of others – in the name of never ageing. But when Victorian society raged at Dorian’s monstrosity, Wilde countered that “vice and virtue are to the artist materials for an art” that can reveal humanity to itself. Sure, Dorian was a perverted Peter Pan, a bad boy who didn’t want to grow up and face consequences. But his scandalous romp reflected society’s concealed desires back to itself.

In fin-de-siècle decadence, we can also see a growing appreciation of female desire. The 1892 poetry collection Sight and Song by Michael Field – the pen name of two lesbian lovers who wrote as one – turns an explicitly female gaze on the art-historical canon. A poem in response to Leonardo da Vinci’s drawing of Leda, the princess seduced by Zeus in the form of a swan, grants Leda all the power: “She draws the fondled creature to her will.” Their Saint Sebastian is, by contrast, a passive icon of masculine beauty, “with body fresh for use, for pleasure fit, / With its energies and needs together knit”.

So too have Black and postcolonial artists drawn from late-19th-century decadence in asserting their own claims to pleasure. Bruce Nugent’s homoerotic story Smoke, Lilies and Jade (1926), one of the more audacious works of the Harlem Renaissance, opens with the Black hero, Alex, lying on his bed, exhaling blue smoke from a cigarette. Alex idly ponders Wilde’s remark that “a cigarette is the most perfect pleasure because it leaves one unsatisfied” before passing into the streets in search of more gratifying pleasures. He meets a white man he calls Beauty, and the two embrace: Alex “could feel Beauty’s body … close against his … hot … tense … white … and soft”. That sentence’s panting prose gives away the game – Alex knows that enjoying the pleasure forbidden to him is the ultimate decadent act.

And now? A renewed, democratic decadence could stage a revolt against optimisation, encouraging ordinary people to brace themselves against the siren simulations of the digital world. Because contemporary culture looks decadent but feels punishing and devoid of meaning, a New Decadence could respond powerfully to this essential contradiction. Every day acts of aesthetic perception – such as Walter Pater stopping traffic to stroke a cat – matter. But if a New Decadence is to emerge, we need artists to invent it and individuals to pause and appreciate its disruptive energies.

So far, neodecadent energies in art have been submerged in satirical entertainments about rich people behaving badly – films like Saltburn or TV shows like The White Lotus that reproduce the structure of pleasureless decadence by equating pleasure with status, power and consumption.

There are signs, however, of something more original and less reactive emerging, an art that foregrounds the senses for an era that distrusts the body. The sensuous cinema of Peter Strickland; the frightening but gorgeous blood-coloured sculptures of Anish Kapoor; the reinvigoration of Black decadence in Shola von Reinhold’s novel Lote; the Dionysian reimagining of the fin de siècle in John Corigliano’s opera The Lord of Cries – none of this amounts to a coherent movement. Yet all these works offer, to their respective artforms, materials from which a New Decadence could arise – a movement that could give pleasure back to people, make the social body’s pulses race again, and force fresh blood through today’s complacent, anemic culture.

Walter Pater prefaced his study of the Renaissance with a sort of epicurean pleasure script, a series of diagnostic questions you can ask yourself to get a better handle on what you experience:

What is this song or picture, this engaging personality presented in life or in a book, to me? What effect does it really produce on me? Does it give me pleasure? and if so, what sort or degree of pleasure? How is my nature modified by its presence, and under its influence?

Your answers to these questions, he argues, have the virtue of satisfying your soul. Giving your attention to what you are feeling, analyzing your impressions, being moved and attentive to life’s everyday experiences – this is where real pleasure lies, so long as your pleasure harms no one else’s.

Why strive for pleasure? Why long for it? Because – contra the Bryan Johnsons of the world – we will die. “A counted number of pulses only,” Pater writes, “is given to us of a variegated, dramatic life.” Like Johnson, like the humanmaxxers, Pater counts his pulses. “Our one chance lies,” he writes, “in expanding that interval, in getting as many pulsations as possible into the given time.”

How different Pater’s pulse-counting is from that of the biometric ascetics. Against the pressure to optimise life, decadence issues a different command: feel it.

In contrast, today’s anhedonic decadence celebrates the inhibition, even the transcendence, of appetite. While in haute cuisine the trappings of indulgence are preserved – some upmarket eateries now offer “small appetite” menus featuring caviar and foie gras – the tendency is toward delicate minimalism. Because eating is a quintessentially communal activity, an intervention in how people eat is also an intervention in how we socialize.It seems reasonable to expect, meanwhile, that the widespread uptake of such drugs may contribute to a tightening not just of belts but of beauty norms. Looksmaxxing, an online subculture aimed primarily at young men, presents a darker strain of physical perfectionism, treating the body as a site of correction. Of course, women have long been ground down by painful and impossible beauty standards. What’s striking about looksmaxxing is the migration of this kind of disciplinary logic into a male subculture that speaks of beauty in terms of brutal domination: anyone can be “mogged” (outshone by a more handsome man), and one of the purposes of maxxing is to increase one’s “sexual market value”. Key to this subculture is the rejection of subjective taste in favor of mathematical norms (looksmaxxers prize certain ratios of facial proportion, measuring, for instance, the height of the forehead or the distance between the pupils).“[T]o make oneself beautiful is a universal instinct,” a young Max Beerbohm wrote in his 1894 essay A Defence of Cosmetics, a send-up of decadence’s cult of artifice. Whereas the fin-de-siècle decadents with their love of makeup treated the face as a mask to play with or an enigma to contemplate, looksmaxxers recast the face as a set of homogenizing metrics requiring arduous correction. “The men are weeping in the gym,” writes Andrew McMillan in his prescient 2015 poem about punitive male beauty standards: they have got too close to the glass and now they are laying in the broken pools of their own faces. The pleasureless decadence machineThe fin de siècle had its own cult of masculine self-display in the form of the dandy, with his carefully tailored coat, polished shoes and pigskin gloves. The dandy’s concern for appearance was just part of the era’s wide-ranging love of stylization. “The first duty in life is to be as artificial as possible,” Oscar Wilde proclaimed. “What the second duty is no one has yet discovered.” Wilde and other decadents prized the made over the natural. Artifice was a way of intensifying the given world, overlaying the hard facts of life with a glittering sheen or a more pleasant smell. After all, what is the dandy’s perfume but a victory for pleasure over necessity?AI marks a triumph of artifice more sweeping than the old decadents could have imagined. Yet far from bolstering our capacity for perceptual intensity, AI presents new threats to both. Its productions – LinkedIn posts about the virtues of entrepreneurship, cartoon soap operas about the infidelities of anthropomorphized fruits – are eerily hollow, with no felt experience, embodiment or sensation behind them. AI is the pleasureless decadence machine.Already our algorithmically driven culture is saturated with a deluge of slop that promises numbing, empty stimulation. The old decadents were fascinated by the prospect of mental oblivion, the loss of self-control in the face of overwhelming beauty. Today, AI researchers warn of “human enfeeblement” as tech companies seek to draw users into relations of dependency and infantilization, with machines to do their “thinking” for them.While the fin-de-siècle left imprints on visual art, fashion, music and other art forms, it was primarily as a literary movement that its decadence made cultural interventions. Crucial to decadent writing was a taste for language – lilting rhythms, overheated exclamations – that would affect the reader viscerally, leaving her trembling, her moral assumptions upended. In contrast, LLMs leach language of pleasure by blandifying it: the algorithm steers language away from the idiosyncratic and toward the predictable.Pleasure isn’t just about hedonism or indulgence in “useless” objects. It is one of the principal ways we, as embodied beings, perceive value. Pain teaches us not to touch the hot stove twice; pleasure guides us toward the sweetness of clean water and fresh air. Pleasure is not infallible: some things that feel good are cruel, addictive, or destructive. But the embodied experience of pleasure is crucial to how we learn and how we make judgments about what is good, beautiful and worth pursuing. These are not judgments we can wisely cede to disembodied machines.“There is no pleasure or pain for an AI, no skin in the game,” the philosopher Carissa Véliz writes in her recent book Prophecy. As a result, an AI “cannot care, and therefore cannot value”. Without some felt relation to pleasure and pain, judgments of value and taste become abstract and bloodless.Reclaiming everyday pleasuresBecause of its commitment to embodied pleasure, fin-de-siècle decadence offers powerful lessons for the increasingly disembodied, tech-optimised world championed by elites. This is not to suggest, however, that the old decadents were living uncomplicated lives of satisfaction and joy. WB Yeats called the poets of 1890s London “the tragic generation”. The decadents could be moody and morbid, susceptible to ennui, spleen and other Baudelairean ailments. In other words, they were all too human. Some died young, succumbing to alcoholism or tuberculosis; others abandoned the religion of art to join the Catholic church. Fin-de-siècle decadence had, moreover, an aristocratic and misogynistic bent. Many of its most influential English champions were highly educated men who regarded ordinary life with aloofness, even contempt.From the start, however, decadence was both an elite and a minoritarian movement, spearheaded largely by men (and some women) of privilege – but responsible for injecting a new awareness of queerness into public consciousness.Oscar Wilde’s 1890 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray is a story of a thrill-seeker’s descent into decadent squalor – hedonism, moral bankruptcy, irresponsible self-indulgence and the exploitation of others – in the name of never ageing. But when Victorian society raged at Dorian’s monstrosity, Wilde countered that “vice and virtue are to the artist materials for an art” that can reveal humanity to itself. Sure, Dorian was a perverted Peter Pan, a bad boy who didn’t want to grow up and face consequences. But his scandalous romp reflected society’s concealed desires back to itself.In fin-de-siècle decadence, we can also see a growing appreciation of female desire. The 1892 poetry collection Sight and Song by Michael Field – the pen name of two lesbian lovers who wrote as one – turns an explicitly female gaze on the art-historical canon. A poem in response to Leonardo da Vinci’s drawing of Leda, the princess seduced by Zeus in the form of a swan, grants Leda all the power: “She draws the fondled creature to her will.” Their Saint Sebastian is, by contrast, a passive icon of masculine beauty, “with body fresh for use, for pleasure fit, / With its energies and needs together knit”.Leda and the Swan, 16th century, attributed to the followers of Leonardo da Vinci. Photograph: Heritage Images/Getty ImagesSo too have Black and postcolonial artists drawn from late-19th-century decadence in asserting their own claims to pleasure. Bruce Nugent’s homoerotic story Smoke, Lilies and Jade (1926), one of the more audacious works of the Harlem Renaissance, opens with the Black hero, Alex, lying on his bed, exhaling blue smoke from a cigarette. Alex idly ponders Wilde’s remark that “a cigarette is the most perfect pleasure because it leaves one unsatisfied” before passing into the streets in search of more gratifying pleasures. He meets a white man he calls Beauty, and the two embrace: Alex “could feel Beauty’s body … close against his … hot … tense … white … and soft”. That sentence’s panting prose gives away the game – Alex knows that enjoying the pleasure forbidden to him is the ultimate decadent act.And now? A renewed, democratic decadence could stage a revolt against optimisation, encouraging ordinary people to brace themselves against the siren simulations of the digital world. Because contemporary culture looks decadent but feels punishing and devoid of meaning, a New Decadence could respond powerfully to this essential contradiction. Every day acts of aesthetic perception – such as Walter Pater stopping traffic to stroke a cat – matter. But if a New Decadence is to emerge, we need artists to invent it and individuals to pause and appreciate its disruptive energies.So far, neodecadent energies in art have been submerged in satirical entertainments about rich people behaving badly – films like Saltburn or TV shows like The White Lotus that reproduce the structure of pleasureless decadence by equating pleasure with status, power and consumption.There are signs, however, of something more original and less reactive emerging, an art that foregrounds the senses for an era that distrusts the body. The sensuous cinema of Peter Strickland; the frightening but gorgeous blood-coloured sculptures of Anish Kapoor; the reinvigoration of Black decadence in Shola von Reinhold’s novel Lote; the Dionysian reimagining of the fin de siècle in John Corigliano’s opera The Lord of Cries – none of this amounts to a coherent movement. Yet all these works offer, to their respective artforms, materials from which a New Decadence could arise – a movement that could give pleasure back to people, make the social body’s pulses race again, and force fresh blood through today’s complacent, anemic culture.A gallery worker poses with the work Mount Moriah at the Gate of the Ghetto by Anish Kapoor at the Hayward Gallery in London on 15 June 2026. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAWalter Pater prefaced his study of the Renaissance with a sort of epicurean pleasure script, a series of diagnostic questions you can ask yourself to get a better handle on what you experience: What is this song or picture, this engaging personality presented in life or in a book, to me? What effect does it really produce on me? Does it give me pleasure? and if so, what sort or degree of pleasure? How is my nature modified by its presence, and under its influence? Your answers to these questions, he argues, have the virtue of satisfying your soul. Giving your attention to what you are feeling, analyzing your impressions, being moved and attentive to life’s everyday experiences – this is where real pleasure lies, so long as your pleasure harms no one else’s.Why strive for pleasure? Why long for it? Because – contra the Bryan Johnsons of the world – we will die. “A counted number of pulses only,” Pater writes, “is given to us of a variegated, dramatic life.” Like Johnson, like the humanmaxxers, Pater counts his pulses. “Our one chance lies,” he writes, “in expanding that interval, in getting as many pulsations as possible into the given time.”How different Pater’s pulse-counting is from that of the biometric ascetics. Against the pressure to optimise life, decadence issues a different command: feel it..

blocks.html_en: The concept of decadence as a marker of cultural decline coinciding with a high level of wealth has been around since the twilight of the ancient Greeks and Romans. After the Roman emperor Elagabalus took the throne at 14, he served flamingo brains, seasoned his food with pearls, and, according to one account, smothered guests to death with an avalanche of rose petals. But his vices were outdone by Nero, who had his enemies sewn into wild animal skins and devoured by dogs in an elaborate garden spectacle.

blocks.html_en: So decadence has an inescapably pejorative ring, suggesting decay, excess and a falling away from norms and ideals. Critics of decadence have usually hailed from the political right, and the same is true today: consider conservative New York Times columnist Ross Douthat’s critique of cultural and economic stagnation in his 2020 book The Decadent Society, or billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s complaints about faltering innovation and the supposed decline of the west. JD Vance likes to invoke the fall of Rome, warning, in his 2026 memoir Communion, that the US is “a great civilization” tumbling into “disrepair”. But plenty of thinkers on the left also worry that modern wealthy societies have entered a period of paralysis, under the shadow of what the Italian theorist Franco “Bifo” Berardi calls “the slow cancellation of the future”.

Cultures later judged decadent produced extraordinary upwellings of art, like the flare of a dying star. Think of the undulating arabesques of Rococo painting before the French Revolution, or the lush shimmering silks of the late Ottomans, or the experimental cinema and nightlife of Weimar Berlin.

blocks.html_en: Nowhere was the cultural potential of decadence more visible than in the late-19th century. In France, Britain and (with less gusto) in the United States, artists such as Oscar Wilde, Aubrey Beardsley, Joris-Karl Huysmans and Rachilde developed new literary and visual styles championing extravagance, sensuousness and the superiority of artifice. It is to these avant-garde experiments that we owe green carnations (the fakest of flowers), frivolous dandies obsessed with perfumes, a bejeweled tortoise crushed to death by the weight of its splendor, and erotic nightmares including a woman with monstrous flowers growing between her thighs and a male anatomical model whose legs spread at the click of a spring so that he can be penetrated by his female lover. Such taboo-busting grotesquery protested against the inertia of modern civilization by applying moral and aesthetic shock treatment.

blocks.html_en: The decadents, however, were not just provocateurs. Their revolt against Victorian society’s deadening enslavement to usefulness, materialism and conventionality put forward a positive philosophy of life, a certain way of thinking about pleasure. Against their era’s obsession with use-value and profit, the decadents insisted that pleasure was, or ought to be, “useless”, enjoyed for its own sake in life’s passing moments. “Not the fruit of experience, but experience itself, is the end,” intoned the essayist Walter Pater, one of the guiding lights of English decadence, in his masterpiece The Renaissance. A reclusive Oxford don, Pater was said to have once stopped High Street traffic to stroke a cat. Why? For the sensation of fur beneath his fingers. The virtue of decadent pleasure is that it is useless, an end in itself.

blocks.html_en: The problem with contemporary culture isn’t that we’re too decadent. We have inherited the surfaces of decadence – luxury, excess, artifice, bodily display – but have surrendered the fin de siècle’s commitment to pleasure. The result is a culture in which pleasure is subordinated to programs of optimisation and replaced at scale by numbing algorithmic stimulation and promises of instant gratification. Whether you’re after goods, food, art or ideas, you can get more, faster, now.

blocks.html_en: Bryan Johnson, the frequently shirtless tech tycoon who has funnelled his fortune into what he calls the “Don’t Die” movement, has turned his quest for immortality into a prolonged exhibition of ascetic self-management. His lifestyle is harrowingly spartan: he doesn’t drink alcohol, avoids the sun, never goes out in the evening, and subsists primarily on lentils, boiled broccoli and macadamia nuts. Yet his regimen is, in its peculiar way, one of prurient excess. He swallows up to 111 pills a day, tracks his night-time erections, and once tapped his teenage son for blood plasma. His fight against death costs a reported $2m a year.

blocks.html_en: Like Johnson, des Esseintes is medically fragile, obsessed with death, and preoccupied with the minutiae of his private sensations. Like Johnson, he sees his retreat from ordinary society into a tightly controlled artificial environment as an experiment that tests the limits of human possibility. But whereas des Esseintes’s withdrawal is an immersion into the subtleties of sensation, Johnson’s “Don’t Die” movement treats the delights of the senses as suspect, even fatal. Des Esseintes hosts a funeral banquet for his “dead virility” in a dining room draped in black, opening on to charcoaled gardens, with guests dining on black-bordered plates filled with black food (rye bread, caviar, black pudding, cuts of meat dripping with liquorice-coloured sauce). Johnson, by contrast, treats impotence as a technical problem, repeatedly shocking his penis to increase his erections.

blocks.html_en: In contexts of extreme inequality, rich people tend to set the terms by which pleasure is understood and experienced. The very fact of inequality injures pleasure, because in a stratified society, food, art, travel and other delights can devolve into occasions to demonstrate rank or taste. Our present social order, however, is not just radically unequal; it’s dominated by a ruling class that distrusts pleasure and sensation. What passes for “fun” among today’s top 0.001% amounts to anything but: think of the 80-hour workweeks championed by tech titans like Elon Musk, or Equinox gym’s “Optimize” longevity membership costing $40,000 a year, or courtside seats at Knicks games inside the miniature surveillance state that is Madison Square Garden. blocks.html_en: The decadence of the fin de siècle celebrated cornucopian abundance. Take for example Aubrey Beardsley’s 1896 drawing The Fruit Bearers, depicting two figures bearing colossal bowls of fruit, lush grapes overhanging, a peacock in the background observing the opulent procession. In contrast, today’s anhedonic decadence celebrates the inhibition, even the transcendence, of appetite. While in haute cuisine the trappings of indulgence are preserved – some upmarket eateries now offer “small appetite” menus featuring caviar and foie gras – the tendency is toward delicate minimalism. Because eating is a quintessentially communal activity, an intervention in how people eat is also an intervention in how we socialize.

blocks.html_en: It seems reasonable to expect, meanwhile, that the widespread uptake of such drugs may contribute to a tightening not just of belts but of beauty norms. Looksmaxxing, an online subculture aimed primarily at young men, presents a darker strain of physical perfectionism, treating the body as a site of correction. Of course, women have long been ground down by painful and impossible beauty standards. What’s striking about looksmaxxing is the migration of this kind of disciplinary logic into a male subculture that speaks of beauty in terms of brutal domination: anyone can be “mogged” (outshone by a more handsome man), and one of the purposes of maxxing is to increase one’s “sexual market value”. blocks.html_en: The fin de siècle had its own cult of masculine self-display in the form of the dandy, with his carefully tailored coat, polished shoes and pigskin gloves. The dandy’s concern for appearance was just part of the era’s wide-ranging love of stylization. “The first duty in life is to be as artificial as possible,” Oscar Wilde proclaimed. “What the second duty is no one has yet discovered.” Wilde and other decadents prized the made over the natural. Artifice was a way of intensifying the given world, overlaying the hard facts of life with a glittering sheen or a more pleasant smell. After all, what is the dandy’s perfume but a victory for pleasure over necessity?

blocks.html_en: AI marks a triumph of artifice more sweeping than the old decadents could have imagined. Yet far from bolstering our capacity for perceptual intensity, AI presents new threats to both. Its productions – LinkedIn posts about the virtues of entrepreneurship, cartoon soap operas about the infidelities of anthropomorphized fruits – are eerily hollow, with no felt experience, embodiment or sensation behind them. AI is the pleasureless decadence machine.

blocks.html_en: Already our algorithmically driven culture is saturated with a deluge of slop that promises numbing, empty stimulation. The old decadents were fascinated by the prospect of mental oblivion, the loss of self-control in the face of overwhelming beauty. Today, AI researchers warn of “human enfeeblement” as tech companies seek to draw users into relations of dependency and infantilization, with machines to do their “thinking” for them.

blocks.html_en: While the fin-de-siècle left imprints on visual art, fashion, music and other art forms, it was primarily as a literary movement that its decadence made cultural interventions. Crucial to decadent writing was a taste for language – lilting rhythms, overheated exclamations – that would affect the reader viscerally, leaving her trembling, her moral assumptions upended. In contrast, LLMs leach language of pleasure by blandifying it: the algorithm steers language away from the idiosyncratic and toward the predictable.

blocks.html_en: Pleasure isn’t just about hedonism or indulgence in “useless” objects. It is one of the principal ways we, as embodied beings, perceive value. Pain teaches us not to touch the hot stove twice; pleasure guides us toward the sweetness of clean water and fresh air. Pleasure is not infallible: some things that feel good are cruel, addictive, or destructive. But the embodied experience of pleasure is crucial to how we learn and how we make judgments about what is good, beautiful and worth pursuing. These are not judgments we can wisely cede to disembodied machines.

blocks.html_en: Because of its commitment to embodied pleasure, fin-de-siècle decadence offers powerful lessons for the increasingly disembodied, tech-optimised world championed by elites. This is not to suggest, however, that the old decadents were living uncomplicated lives of satisfaction and joy. WB Yeats called the poets of 1890s London “the tragic generation”. The decadents could be moody and morbid, susceptible to ennui, spleen and other Baudelairean ailments. In other words, they were all too human. Some died young, succumbing to alcoholism or tuberculosis; others abandoned the religion of art to join the Catholic church. Fin-de-siècle decadence had, moreover, an aristocratic and misogynistic bent. Many of its most influential English champions were highly educated men who regarded ordinary life with aloofness, even contempt.

blocks.html_en: Oscar Wilde’s 1890 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray is a story of a thrill-seeker’s descent into decadent squalor – hedonism, moral bankruptcy, irresponsible self-indulgence and the exploitation of others – in the name of never ageing. But when Victorian society raged at Dorian’s monstrosity, Wilde countered that “vice and virtue are to the artist materials for an art” that can reveal humanity to itself. Sure, Dorian was a perverted Peter Pan, a bad boy who didn’t want to grow up and face consequences. But his scandalous romp reflected society’s concealed desires back to itself.

blocks.html_en: In fin-de-siècle decadence, we can also see a growing appreciation of female desire. The 1892 poetry collection Sight and Song by Michael Field – the pen name of two lesbian lovers who wrote as one – turns an explicitly female gaze on the art-historical canon. A poem in response to Leonardo da Vinci’s drawing of Leda, the princess seduced by Zeus in the form of a swan, grants Leda all the power: “She draws the fondled creature to her will.” Their Saint Sebastian is, by contrast, a passive icon of masculine beauty, “with body fresh for use, for pleasure fit, / With its energies and needs together knit”.

blocks.html_en: So too have Black and postcolonial artists drawn from late-19th-century decadence in asserting their own claims to pleasure. Bruce Nugent’s homoerotic story Smoke, Lilies and Jade (1926), one of the more audacious works of the Harlem Renaissance, opens with the Black hero, Alex, lying on his bed, exhaling blue smoke from a cigarette. Alex idly ponders Wilde’s remark that “a cigarette is the most perfect pleasure because it leaves one unsatisfied” before passing into the streets in search of more gratifying pleasures. He meets a white man he calls Beauty, and the two embrace: Alex “could feel Beauty’s body … close against his … hot … tense … white … and soft”. That sentence’s panting prose gives away the game – Alex knows that enjoying the pleasure forbidden to him is the ultimate decadent act.

对于任何拥有互联网连接和少量可自由支配收入的人来说，当代时刻提供了大量诱人的干扰。 那么为什么空虚的情绪无处不在呢？ 为什么这么多人同时感到过度刺激和无聊？

欢迎来到没有享乐的颓废时代。

自古希腊人和古罗马人的黄昏以来，颓废的概念就一直存在，作为文化衰落与高财富水平同时发生的标志。 罗马皇帝埃拉加巴卢斯 (Elagabalus) 14 岁即位后，他用火烈鸟大脑招待客人，用珍珠调味，而且根据一种说法，他还用雪崩般的玫瑰花瓣将客人闷死。 但他的恶习被尼禄所超越，尼禄将他的敌人缝进野生动物皮中，并在精心设计的花园奇观中被狗吞掉。

因此，颓废不可避免地带有贬义，暗示着腐朽、过度以及背离规范和理想。 对颓废的批评通常来自政治右翼，今天也是如此：想想保守派《纽约时报》专栏作家罗斯·杜塔特 (Ross Douthat) 在其 2020 年出版的《颓废社会》一书中对文化和经济停滞的批评，或者亿万富翁投资者彼得·蒂尔 (Peter Thiel) 对创新步履蹒跚和所谓的西方衰落的抱怨。 JD 万斯喜欢援引罗马的衰落，在他 2026 年的回忆录《圣餐》中警告说，美国是“一个伟大的文明”，正陷入“失修”。 但许多左翼思想家也担心，在意大利理论家佛朗哥·“比佛”·贝拉尔迪所说的“未来的缓慢取消”的阴影下，现代富裕社会已经进入瘫痪期。

这一切听起来都很糟糕。 然而，热情的少数人有时会在颓废中找到希望的理由。 后来被判定为颓废的文化产生了非凡的艺术涌动，就像垂死的恒星的耀斑一样。 想想法国大革命前洛可可绘画中起伏的阿拉伯式花纹，或者奥斯曼帝国晚期华丽闪闪发光的丝绸，或者魏玛柏林的实验电影和夜生活。

颓废的文化潜力在 19 世纪末最为明显。 在法国、英国和（热情不那么高的）美国，奥斯卡·王尔德、奥布里·比尔兹利、乔里斯·卡尔·休斯曼和拉柴尔德等艺术家发展了新的文学和视觉风格，崇尚奢华、感性和技巧的优越性。 正是这些前卫的实验，让我们看到了绿色康乃馨（最假的花）、痴迷于香水的轻浮纨绔子弟、一只被其辉煌压死的镶满珠宝的乌龟，以及色情噩梦，包括一个大腿间长着怪异花朵的女人和一个男性解剖模型，他的双腿在弹簧的咔哒声中张开，以便他可以被他的女性情人插入。 这种打破禁忌的怪诞行为，以道德和审美的震撼处理来抗议现代文明的惰性。

然而，颓废派不仅仅是挑衅者。 他们对维多利亚社会对有用性、唯物主义和传统的日益奴役的反抗，提出了一种积极的生活哲学，一种思考快乐的特定方式。 与他们那个时代对使用价值和利润的痴迷相反，颓废派坚持认为快乐是或应该是“无用的”，在生命的逝去时刻为了它本身而享受。 “终点不是经验的果实，而是经验本身，”散文家沃尔特·佩特（Walter Pater）在他的杰作《文艺复兴》中吟诵道，他是英国颓废的指路明灯之一。 佩特是一位隐居的牛津大学教授，据说他曾经阻止大街交通去抚摸一只猫。 为什么？ 为了手指下毛皮的感觉。 颓废快乐的优点在于它是无用的，其本身就是目的。

启发奥斯卡·王尔德和他的同伴的世纪末颓废的迷恋仍然存在于我们身边，但以枯萎的、技术介导的形式存在。 GLP-1 将饮食的乐趣变成了需要解决的问题。 抗衰老疗法和“外观最大化”将颓废对自我造型的关注转变为一种（字面上痛苦的）自我优化形式。 人工智能通过将人类思维外包给一个健谈、渴望取悦的机器管家，重现了颓废派对诡计的热爱。

当代文化的问题不在于我们太颓废。 我们继承了颓废的表面——奢华、过度、诡计、身体展示——但放弃了世纪末对享乐的承诺。 其结果是形成了一种文化，在这种文化中，快乐服从于优化程序，并被麻木的算法刺激和即时满足的承诺大规模取代。 无论您想要商品、食物、艺术还是创意，您现在都可以更快、更多地获得。

但数量和速度无法弥补当今颓废的核心悖论：事实上，它常常“乏味”，而且奇怪地毫无乐趣。 今年春天，亚马逊的中国竞争对手在英国和欧洲推出了一个承诺提供情感满足的名字：Joybuy，这是时代的标志。

“外观最大化”时代

布莱恩·约翰逊 (Bryan Johnson) 是一位经常光着膀子的科技大亨，他将自己的财富投入到了他所谓的“不死”运动中，他将对永生的追求变成了长期的禁欲式自我管理。 他的生活方式极其简朴：不喝酒，避免日晒，晚上从不出门，主要靠扁豆、煮西兰花和澳洲坚果为生。 然而，他的养生方式以其独特的方式，是一种淫荡的放纵行为。 他每天吞下多达 111 粒药片，记录他夜间的勃起情况，并曾经给他十几岁的儿子采集血浆。 据报道，他与死亡的斗争每年花费 200 万美元。

约翰逊将自己描绘成一个未来的人，但他有一个 19 世纪的双重身份。 虽然在颓废文学中，面色苍白、略显雌雄同体、有钱有怪癖的男人并不罕见，但最著名的是让·德埃森特公爵，他是乔里斯·卡尔·于斯曼 1884 年小说《反对谷物》中的英雄，这部作品被认为是颓废的圣经。 作为法国贵族家庭的最后一个后裔，德埃桑特为自己创造了一个充满性感技巧的隐世世界：软垫墙壁、珍本书籍、异国情调的鲜花、芬芳的糖果、微妙的利口酒、甜得近乎腐臭的香水。

和约翰逊一样，德埃桑特在医学上也很脆弱，对死亡着迷，并且全神贯注于他私人感觉的细节。 和约翰逊一样，他将自己从普通社会撤退到严格控制的人工环境中视为测试人类可能性极限的实验。 然而，德埃森特的退出是一种沉浸在感觉的微妙之处，约翰逊的“不死”运动则将感官的愉悦视为可疑，甚至是致命的。 德埃森特在一间铺着黑色窗帘的餐厅里为他的“死去的男子气概”举办了一场葬礼宴会，餐厅通向炭火燃烧的花园，客人们在装满黑色食物的黑边盘子上用餐（黑麦面包、鱼子酱、黑布丁、滴着甘草色酱汁的肉片）。 相比之下，约翰逊将阳痿视为一个技术问题，反复电击他的阴茎以增加勃起。

约翰逊的计划很极端，但他并非特例。 他的生活方式以夸张的形式展现了当今科技亿万富翁对快乐和体现的新态度。 虽然帕洛阿尔托及其周边地区的一些超级富豪在礼宾医生的帮助下通过生物黑客技术来延长寿命，但其他人甚至将性快感视为可以通过医疗干预来完善的领域。 例如，在莎莉·格林沃尔德博士的独家妇产科诊所，绰号为“亿万富翁的阴道俱乐部”——格林沃尔德将她的客户描述为“前 0.001%”——中年女性可以通过定制建议、荷尔蒙鸡尾酒和跟踪设备来提高她们的“性寿命”。 “性爱等于睡眠、减轻压力、心血管参与、关系满足和盆底健康，而这些都等于健康，”格林沃尔德说。

这些态度反映了一小部分精英的幻想，他们痴迷于人类的进步，尤其是延长自己的生存时间。 毫无乐趣的颓废的阶级政治可以粗略地概括为：针对富人的生物黑客和量化禁欲主义，针对其他人的算法刺激。

在极端不平等的背景下，富人倾向于设定理解和体验快乐的条件。 不平等的事实本身就损害了快乐，因为在一个分层的社会中，食物、艺术、旅行和其他快乐可能会变成展示等级或品味的场合。 然而，我们目前的社会秩序不仅是根本不平等，而且是不平等的。它由不信任快乐和感觉的统治阶级统治。 当今 0.001% 的顶尖人口中所谓的“乐趣”根本不是：想想埃隆·马斯克等科技巨头所倡导的每周 80 小时工作制，或者 Equinox 健身房每年花费 4 万美元的“优化”长寿会员资格，或者在麦迪逊广场花园的微型监控区域内观看尼克斯队比赛的场边座位。 由于他们巨大的政治和文化影响力，他们对公共和私人投资的影响力，以及他们不缴纳应缴税款的习惯，超级富有阶层的不快感会蔓延到我们其他人身上。

“我认为尝试优化事情...... 德国生物技术亿万富翁克里斯蒂安·安格迈尔 (Christian Angermayer) 最近宣称，他是“HumanMaxxing”（使用药物和补充剂来增强身体）的倡导者。 撇开神性不谈，似乎有必要提及的是，满足于日常感觉的人是一个贫穷的消费者。 但如果让富豪阶层之外的人重新认识自己的思想和身体，将其视为永恒的自我完善的场所，用安格梅尔的话说，你就拥有了“理想情况下 100% 的潜在市场”。

最具文化内涵的此类市场是 Ozempic、Wegovy 和 Mounjaro 等 GLP-1。 根据 2025 年盖洛普民意调查，八分之一的美国成年人表示服用 GLP-1 注射剂来减肥，而且更多人表示有兴趣服用。 到 2035 年，此类药物的全球市场预计将达到 1900 亿美元。 对于许多人来说，这些药物带来了真正的好处。 然而，我们似乎可以公平地问：控制食欲药物的广泛使用表明我们的文化如何处理愉悦和欲望？

正如研究已经开始表明的那样，GLP-1 重塑了欲望和满足感之间的感觉关系。 虽然还需要更多的研究，但一些用户报告说，他们生活的几个方面的快乐感减少了：他们抱怨嗜睡、性欲下降、情绪平淡以及与饮食的社会层面的联系减弱。

世纪末的颓废庆祝了聚宝盆的丰富。 以奥布里·比尔兹利 (Aubrey Beardsley) 1896 年的画作《水果持有者》(The Fruit Bearers) 为例，画中两个人物端着巨大的水果碗，悬垂着茂盛的葡萄，背景中一只孔雀观察着华丽的游行队伍。 相比之下，今天的快感匮乏的颓废庆祝了食欲的抑制，甚至是超越。 虽然高级美食保留了放纵的装饰——一些高档餐馆现在提供以鱼子酱和鹅肝为特色的“小胃口”菜单——但趋势是精致的极简主义。 因为饮食本质上是一种公共活动，所以对人们饮食方式的干预也是对我们社交方式的干预。

与此同时，我们似乎可以合理地预期，此类药物的广泛使用可能不仅会导致人们勒紧腰带，还会导致美容规范。 Looksmaxxing 是一种主要针对年轻男性的在线亚文化，呈现出一种更黑暗的身体完美主义倾向，将身体视为矫正的场所。 当然，女性长期以来一直被痛苦且不可能的美丽标准所压垮。 颜值最大化的惊人之处在于，这种规训逻辑迁移到了男性亚文化中，这种亚文化用残酷的统治来谈论美：任何人都可以被“蒙蔽”（被更帅的男人盖过），而颜值最大化的目的之一就是增加一个人的“性市场价值”。 这种亚文化的关键是拒绝主观品味，转而采用数学规范（lookmaxxers 重视特定的面部比例，例如测量前额的高度或瞳孔之间的距离）。

“让自己变得美丽是一种普遍的本能，”年轻的马克斯·比尔博姆 (Max Beerbohm) 在他 1894 年的文章《化妆品的辩护》中写道，该文讽刺了颓废派对诡计的崇拜。 世纪末的颓废派热爱化妆，将脸部视为玩弄的面具或思考的谜团，而造型美化者则将脸部重新塑造为一组需要艰苦校正的同质化指标。 “男人们在健身房里哭泣，”安德鲁·麦克米伦 (Andrew McMillan) 在他 2015 年关于惩罚性男性审美标准的富有先见之明的诗中写道：

他们离玻璃太近了，现在正躺在自己脸上的破碎的水坑里。

毫无乐趣的颓废机器

世纪末人们对男性自我展示的崇拜以花花公子的形式出现，他们穿着精心剪裁的外套、擦亮的鞋子和猪皮手套。 花花公子对外表的关注只是这个时代对风格化广泛热爱的一部分。 奥斯卡·王尔德宣称：“人生的首要责任就是尽可能做作。” “第二个职责是什么还没有人发现。” 王尔德和其他颓废主义者更看重人造的东西而不是自然的东西。 技巧是强化既定世界的一种方式，用闪闪发光的光泽或更令人愉悦的气味覆盖生活中残酷的事实。 毕竟，花花公子的香水不就是快乐战胜必需品的胜利吗？

人工智能标志着技术的胜利，其影响范围之广超出了旧颓废者的想象。 然而，人工智能远非增强我们感知强度的能力，而是对两者都带来了新的威胁。 它的作品——LinkedIn上关于创业美德的帖子、关于拟人化水果的不忠的卡通肥皂剧——出奇地空洞，背后没有任何可感受到的经验、体现或感觉。 人工智能是毫无乐趣的颓废机器。

我们的算法驱动的文化已经充斥着大量的废液，这些废液会带来麻木、空洞的刺激。 老颓废者着迷于精神遗忘的前景，面对压倒性的美丽而失去自我控制。 如今，人工智能研究人员警告称，科技公司试图让用户陷入依赖和幼稚化的关系，让机器替他们“思考”，这会导致“人类衰弱”。

虽然世纪末在视觉艺术、时尚、音乐和其他艺术形式上留下了印记，但它的颓废主要是作为一场文学运动而对文化进行干预的。 颓废写作的关键是对语言的品味——轻快的节奏、过热的感叹——这会从内心深处影响读者，让她颤抖，她的道德假设被颠覆。 相比之下，法学硕士通过美化语言来滤取愉悦的语言：算法引导语言远离特殊性，转向可预测的。

快乐不仅仅是享乐主义或沉迷于“无用”的物体。 这是我们作为具体存在感知价值的主要方式之一。 痛苦教会我们不要再碰热​​炉；快乐引导我们走向洁净水和新鲜空气的甜蜜。 快乐并非绝对正确：有些感觉良好的事物是残酷的、令人上瘾的或具有破坏​​性的。 但快乐的具体体验对于我们如何学习以及如何判断什么是善、美和值得追求至关重要。 我们不能明智地把这些判断交给无形的机器。

哲学家 Carissa Véliz 在她最近出版的《预言》一书中写道：“对于人工智能来说，没有快乐或痛苦，没有风险。” 结果，人工智能“无法关心，因此无法评估”。 如果没有与快乐和痛苦的某种感觉联系，对价值和品味的判断就会变得抽象和冷漠。

重拾日常乐趣

由于其对具体快乐的承诺，世纪末的颓废为精英所拥护的日益脱离现实、技术优化的世界提供了有力的教训。 然而，这并不是说过去的颓废者过着简单而满足和快乐的生活。 WB Yeats 将 20 世纪 90 年代伦敦的诗人称为“悲剧的一代”。 颓废者可能喜怒无常、病态，容易患上倦怠、脾脏和其他波德莱尔式的疾病。 换句话说，他们都太人性化了。 有些人英年早逝，死于酗酒或肺结核；其他人放弃了艺术宗教，加入了天主教会。 此外，世纪末的颓废还带有贵族气息和厌恶女性的倾向。 许多最有影响力的英国冠军都是受过高等教育的人，他们对平凡的生活感到冷漠，甚至蔑视。

然而，从一开始，颓废既是一场精英运动，又是一场少数派运动，主要由享有特权的男性（和一些女性）带头——但负责将新的酷儿意识注入公众意识。

奥斯卡·王尔德 1890 年的小说《道林·格雷的画像》讲述了一个寻求刺激的人以永不衰老的名义陷入颓废肮脏的故事——享乐主义、道德破产、不负责任的自我放纵和剥削他人。 但当维多利亚社会对多里安的怪物感到愤怒时，王尔德反驳道，“邪恶和美德对于艺术家来说是艺术的材料”，可以向自身揭示人性。 当然，多里安是一个变态的彼得潘，一个不想长大并面对后果的坏男孩。 但他的丑闻反映了社会隐藏的欲望。

在世纪末的颓废中，我们也可以看到对女性欲望的日益欣赏。 迈克尔·菲尔德 (Michael Field) 创作的 1892 年诗集《视觉与歌曲》（这是两位女同性恋恋人合体创作的笔名）将明确的女性视角转向了艺术史经典。 一首诗回应了列奥纳多·达·芬奇所画的勒达，这位被宙斯以天鹅的形式引诱的公主，赋予了勒达所有的力量：“她让被爱抚的生物服从她的意愿。” 相比之下，他们的圣塞巴斯蒂安是男性美的被动象征，“身体新鲜，适合使用，愉悦合身，/其能量和需求交织在一起”。

黑人和后殖民艺术家也从 19 世纪末的颓废中汲取灵感，主张自己对快乐的主张。 布鲁斯·纽金特的同性恋故事《烟、百合与玉》（1926）是哈莱姆文艺复兴时期最大胆的作品之一，开头是黑人英雄亚历克斯躺在床上，呼出香烟的蓝色烟雾。 亚历克斯懒洋洋地思考着王尔德的名言“一支香烟是最完美的快乐，因为它让人不满意”，然后走上街头寻找更令人满意的快乐。 他遇到了一个被他称为“美女”的白人，两人拥抱：亚历克斯“可以感觉到美女的身体...... 紧贴着他的…… 热的 … 紧张…… 白色的 … 且柔软”。 这句话气喘吁吁的散文泄露了游戏的真相——亚历克斯知道享受他所禁止的快乐是终极的颓废行为。

现在呢？ 新的民主颓废可能会引发对优化的反抗，鼓励普通人做好准备，抵御数字世界的海妖模拟。 因为当代文化看起来颓废，但感觉是惩罚性的且缺乏意义，新颓废可以对这一基本矛盾做出强有力的回应。 每天的审美行为——比如沃尔特·佩特（Walter Pater）停下来抚摸一只猫——都很重要。 但如果要出现新的颓废，我们需要艺术家来发明它，需要个人停下来欣赏它的破坏性能量。

到目前为止，艺术中的新颓废主义能量已经淹没在有关富人行为恶劣的讽刺娱乐中——像《盐烧》这样的电影或像《白莲花》这样的电视节目，通过将快乐与地位、权力和消费等同起来，再现了毫无快乐的颓废结构。

然而，有迹象表明，一些更具原创性、更少反应性的东西正在出现，一种在不信任身体的时代突出感官的艺术。 彼得·斯特里克兰的感性电影；安尼什·卡普尔（Anish Kapoor）令人恐惧但华丽的血色雕塑；肖拉·冯·莱因霍尔德的小说《洛特》中黑人颓废的复兴；约翰·科里利亚诺（John Corigliano）的歌剧《哭泣之王》中对世纪末的酒神式重新想象——所有这些都不构成一个连贯的运动。 然而，所有这些作品都为各自的艺术形式提供了可能产生新颓废的材料——一场可以给人们带来快乐的运动，让社会体的脉搏再次加速，并为当今自满、贫血的文化注入新鲜血液。

沃尔特·佩特（Walter Pater）以一种享乐主义的快乐脚本作为他对文艺复兴的研究的序言，这是一系列你可以问自己的诊断问题，以便更好地处理你所经历的事情：

这首歌或这幅画，这在生活或书中呈现的迷人个性对我来说是什么？ 它对我真正产生什么影响？ 它给我带来快乐吗？ 如果是的话，快乐是什么类型或程度？ 我的本性如何因它的存在和影响而改变？

他认为，你对这些问题的回答可以满足你的灵魂。 关注自己的感受，分析自己的印象，感动并关注生活的日常经历——这就是真正的快乐所在，只要你的快乐不伤害别人。

为什么要努力追求快乐？ 为何渴望它？ 因为——与世界上的布莱恩·约翰逊相反——我们会死。 佩特写道：“只有经过计数的脉冲才赋予我们丰富多彩的、戏剧性的生活。” 和约翰逊一样，和人类极限运动者一样，佩特也数着自己的脉搏。 “我们唯一的机会在于，”他写道，“扩大这个间隔，在给定时间内获得尽可能多的脉动。”

佩特的脉搏计数与生物识别苦行僧的脉搏计数有多么不同。 面对优化生活的压力，颓废发出了不同的命令：感受它。
